newsitem.title: UK: S&P affirms Qatar's BBB l-term, A3 s-term ratings.
newsitem.headline: S&P affirms Qatar's BBB l-term, A3 s-term ratings.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Tuesday it affirmed the State of Qatar's BBB long-term and A3 short-term foreign currency ratings.
"The outlook on the ratings is stable," the rating agency said in a statement.
S&P said this affirmation was in connection with Ras Laffan Liquefied Natural Gas Company Ltd's upcoming bond issue.

"The outlook balances the fiscal benefits expected from substantially higher oil and gas output with the challenge of managing a still highly concentrated economy. Moreover, geopolitical risks, which are difficult to predict, could limit upward movement in the rating," S&P said.

"The revenue windfall resulting from rising oil prices should lower the budget deficit to under 5.0 percent of GDP this year and next. However, the government is unlikely to achieve its longer term goal of fiscal balance without a stronger commitment to reduce the size of the public sector," the agency said.
S&P said the ratings were based on Qatar's
-- Large natural gas reserve base, the world's third largest, which is 14 times Qatar's proven oil reserves in equivalent billions of barrels.
-- Modest, but growing, oil reserves, enough to support over two decades of output at current production levels.
-- Responsible economic management, underpinning the development of a modern physical and social infrastructure, and appreciable rise in lining standards over the past two decades.
Per capita income of nearly $13,000 is the highest in the Gulf region after Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates.
-- Financial flexibility afforded by undisclosed, but probably sizable, official foreign assets.
S&P said creditworthiness was constrained by

-- A small, open, and narrowly based economy heavily dependent on oil and gas and exposed to changed in energy prices. High economic concentration heightens the importance of effective management of volatile fiscal revenues and external liquidity as a key rating factor.

-- Fiscal deficits stemming from sizable personnel and defense outlays, and gas-related capital expenditures. The government's debt burden has more than doubled since 1992 to an estimated 58 percent of GDP in 1996.
-- A level of financial disclosure well below that of most other investment-grade sovereigns.
-- Security and event risks posed by long-term domestic political and regional uncertainties, including possible regime changes in neighboring countries.
"These risks are somewhat mitigated by strong diplomatic and military support by the United States and other Western countries," S&P said.

It said the government's large-scale and primarily debt finance investment programme to develop the North Field gas reserves was expected to cost $7.8 billion, $5.0 billion of which would be debt finances.

"Nevertheless, revenues from gas sales --first delivery of which is scheduled for January 1997, and is expected to exceed $1.0 billion in 1998-- should augment and stabilized government revenues, support the growth of gas-related industries, and diversify Qatar's export base," S&P said.

"At the same time, new oil discoveries and the use of enhanced production technologies are expected to extend the life of oil reserves, and raise oil production to over 550,000 barrels per day by 2000," the agency said.
"These, in turn, should narrow budget deficits and reverse growth of the public debt burden longer term," said S&P.
